Threat.value: My body feels constantly tense and ready to react to danger
I feel on guard even inside my own home

Memory.value: Sometimes I can recall what happened but feel completely numb, as if it happened to a stranger
The memory feels like it is happening right now rather than something that is over
When the memory returns I feel so overwhelmed by emotion that I have to stop

Negative Appraisals.value: I will never be able to feel normal emotions again
My body keeps reacting as if I am still in danger even when I am safe
I can no longer trust my own body

issues.explanation: The threat items are oriented toward external environmental danger (scanning surroundings, planning escape routes), which is hard to reconcile with a life-threatening illness trauma in a 68-year-old policy analyst unless there is an additional trauma context not represented here.

Negative Appraisals: Constant Vigilance reinforces an expectation of unpredictable external danger, which fits assault/combat-type trauma more than illness trauma and does not cohere well with the rest of the illness-based profile.

Memory: Guilt on Recall and Negative Appraisals: Character Blame imply a strong self-blame/guilt formulation, but the other selected items center on current danger vigilance and emotional loss; for life-threatening illness, this specific self-blame pattern is possible but, combined with the external-danger threat items, creates a clinically incoherent mix of trauma themes.

For a life-threatening illness trauma, persistent escape-route scanning is hard to reconcile with the trauma context. It implies imminent external attack or entrapment rather than illness-related threat, while the rest of the profile centers on bodily danger and emotional change.

Intense guilt on recall is not impossible after severe illness, but here it sits awkwardly with the rest of the profile: the appraisals focus on permanent emotional loss and bodily alarm rather than responsibility for causing harm or failing others. The guilt theme lacks support elsewhere in memory or appraisals.

'The event happened to me because of the sort of person I am' suggests a strong characterological self-blame formulation. In a life-threatening illness case, that can occur, but in this profile it is not well integrated with the other selected appraisals, which focus on bodily danger and emotional numbing. Together with guilt on recall, it introduces a self-blame theme that is otherwise unsupported.

vignette:
Kwame is a 68-year-old widowed Ghanaian-American man who works as a senior policy analyst for a federal health agency in Washington, D.C. He came to the clinic after months of what he described, with characteristic understatement, as "not being quite right." His PCL-5 score of 77 places him in a range of severe symptom burden, and the picture that emerged across the first several sessions was one of a man whose relationship with his own body had been fundamentally and catastrophically altered.

Approximately fourteen months before his intake appointment, Kwame was admitted to the intensive care unit following a sudden cardiac arrest. He had been at his desk reviewing a legislative brief when the chest pain began - a sensation he initially dismissed as indigestion before it became something else entirely, something vast and crushing that dropped him to the floor of his office. Colleagues found him unresponsive. He was resuscitated twice in the ambulance. In the ICU, he was intubated and sedated for four days, and during the fragmented periods of partial consciousness he retained a visceral, disordered sense of being unable to breathe, of alarms sounding, of hands pressing on his chest, of not knowing whether he was dying or already dead. His wife of thirty-nine years had passed two years prior, and it was his adult daughter who sat at his bedside not knowing whether her father would survive.

He did survive. He was discharged after eleven days, with a defibrillator implanted in his chest and a cardiologist's cautious optimism. For the first several weeks, Kwame moved through his recovery with what appeared to those around him to be composure. He returned calls, attended telehealth appointments, and even submitted a policy brief from home. But something beneath that surface had shifted in a way he could not name and did not yet have language for.

The memory of those hours did not behave like other memories. At times it came back not as something that had happened but as something that was happening - the weight on his sternum, the disorientation, the alarms - arriving with a freshness that made the fourteen months between then and now feel like an illusion. At other times he could think about the hospitalization and feel nothing at all, as though he were reading a case file about a stranger, which disturbed him in a different way. And then there were moments when the memory returned with such emotional force that he had to set down whatever he was doing and simply wait for it to pass.

What frightened Kwame most, he eventually disclosed, was not the memory itself but what the event had revealed about his body. He had come to believe that his body was no longer a reliable instrument - that it had betrayed him once without warning and could do so again at any moment, and that there was nothing he could do to anticipate or prevent it. The defibrillator, which was meant to reassure him, had instead become a symbol of this unreliability. He was certain that the tension he felt throughout his body, the constant low-level readiness that never fully released, was evidence that something remained wrong - that his body was still registering a danger his doctors could not see. He felt this even at home, in his apartment where he had lived for twenty years, where there was no rational threat he could identify. He remained watchful anyway.

At work, the consequences had accumulated quietly. Kwame's role requires him to read dense, complex documents and synthesise them into actionable recommendations, but concentration had become genuinely effortful in a way it had never been before. He had missed two internal deadlines - unprecedented in his career - and had begun arriving earlier and staying later simply to produce the same output, a compensation his colleagues had not yet noticed but that he tracked with quiet shame.

He had also stopped discussing his health with his daughter, deflecting her questions with reassurances he did not believe. He had come to fear that whatever capacity he once had for feeling - the warmth he used to feel talking to her, the satisfaction he used to find in his work - had been damaged in a way that was permanent. What finally brought him to seek help was a moment at his desk when he realised he could not remember the last time he had felt anything he would call ordinary. He came hoping, with great caution, that someone might tell him he was wrong about that.
